Verifying turbulence model reduction in high β tokamak plasmas

High ratio of kinetic to magnetic pressure, β, is a signature of good performance and hence desirable in tokamak
plasmas. Optimizing plasma operation towards high β requires the integration of sources and transport physics modules
in integrated modelling frameworks. Turbulent fluxes, which dominate the transport, are modelled using physics based
reduced quasilinear model like TGLF1. The ability of TGLF to accurately predict turbulent transport at high β is
assessed in a comparison against the higher fidelity gyrokinetic code GKW2. The comparison is performed for an
idealised case and for a JET-based high β case. The linear response of TGLF is verified and improved to better capture
electromagnetic Kinetic Ballooning Modes. The quasi-linear fluxes computed with TGLF match within 75% the non-
linear heat and particle fluxes computed with GKW for the component carried by electric potential fluctuations. The
magnetic flutter component, however, is strongly underestimated. This study indicates that further improvements of
the linear solver and refined saturation rules are needed to properly describe high-β electromagnetic turbulence. The
general trends and thresholds with respect to the driving gradients are nevertheless captured. With these limitations
in mind and using the recommended settings to properly describe Kinetic Ballooning Modes, TGLF can be used in
integrated modelling to explore high-β regimes.
I.
INTRODUCTION
In high plasma β tokamaks, where the ratio of kinetic
to magnetic pressure is significant, electromagnetic modes
known as Kinetic Ballooning Modes (KBMs) can be driven
unstable by the pressure gradient in the bad curvature region.
Since their first description3, KBM theory has been an active
area of research4–12. Initially, KBMs were primarily studied
in the context of pedestal regions13–15. However, recent re-
search has increasingly focused on their role in the core re-
gions of high β tokamaks plasmas, in particular at low mag-
netic shear16–20.
For instance, experimental studies in the
core of DIII-D high performance plasmas point at KBMs as
key players in the regulation of internal transport barriers21.
Quasilinear estimates showed that the KBM-induced fluxes
are consistent with experimental measurements, suggesting
that KBMs are crucial in self-regulating plasma in high β sce-
narios. Furthermore, KBMs have been predicted to be unsta-
ble in the core of JET hybrid H-mode discharges, which are
relevant to ITER’s high β plasmas16,18. The study of KBMs
is crucial for understanding transport in these critical regions
and for the development of predictive models for future fusion
devices22–24. High-fidelity gyrokinetic simulations have been
instrumental to provide insights into the nonlinear evolution of
KBMs, revealing the critical role of zonal flows and nonlinear
mode coupling in regulating KBM turbulence25,26. A notable
study analysed turbulent transport and zonal flow dynamics
in mixed KBM and ion temperature gradient (ITG) mode-
dominated turbulence using gyrokinetic simulations based on
experimental observations from the HL-2A tokamak27. That
study revealed that KBMs and ITGs are the main contribu-
tors to turbulent transport in these scenarios. Nonlinear simu-
lations indicated that at higher β values, the transition from
ITG to KBM-dominated turbulence increases transport de-
spite stronger zonal flows. While non-linear gyrokinetic sim-
ulations are useful to capture and analyse the complex dy-
namics of KBM turbulence, they are too expensive to be used
in integrated modelling frameworks. The computational cost
of nonlinear gyrokinetic simulations, such as those performed
with the GKW code2, is significant, requiring over 105 CPU
hours for a single radial position at one time step. As a re-
sult, there is a strong motivation to develop and validate re-
duced models, like the quasi-linear code TGLF1,28, that offer a
significant reduction in computational cost, averaging around
10 CPU-seconds per simulation, and making them suitable
for integrated modeling frameworks.
Recent research has
benchmarked quasi-linear models like QuaLiKiz29 and TGLF
against high-fidelity gyrokinetic simulations for a high β JET
hybrid discharge17. It demonstrated that while both models
can reproduce certain linear and nonlinear characteristics of
the turbulence, significant differences remain, especially re-
garding the isotope effect and the influence of electromagnetic
stabilization. This study was performed around mid-radius, in
a region close to , but below, the KBM threshold.
The present study aims to benchmark the TGLF reduced
model against the higher-fidelity GKW code to evaluate its ef-
fectiveness in capturing KBMs in high β regimes, especially
at low magnetic shear, close to the magnetic axis. GKW has
been benchmarked against other gyrokinetic codes, such as
GS230 and GENE31 in many occasions2,32,33. By comparing
TGLF with GKW in this study, we aim to understand the lim-
itations and capabilities of TGLF in capturing KBMs, which
are critical for accurate turbulent transport predictions in inte-
grated modeling frameworks. All results are presented using
IMAS normalizations for local gyrokinetic simulations34.
II.
METHODOLOGY
Our goal is to verify the reduced electromagnetic quasi-
linear model TGLF extensively used within integrated mod-
elling. In particular we want to assess its accuracy in the high


2
β regime. The verification is done against the higher fidelity
code GKW solving the gyrokinetic system of equations for-
mulated in the δ f local limit (flux-tube). The GKW code
solves these equations directly, as an initial value problem,
to predict the non-linear evolution of the system and the cor-
responding turbulent fluxes. It can also run linearly to deter-
mine the most unstable eigenmode. The Trapped Gyro Lan-
dau Fluid (TGLF) code solves instead a system of equations
based on velocity space moments of the linear gyrokinetic
equations. In addition, it relies on the quasi-linear approx-
imation to estimate the non-linear turbulent fluxes from the
linear response. Other differences with respect to GKW in-
clude a simplified collision operator (electron-ion pitch angle
scattering), the neglect of centrifugal effects (particles drifts
due to the toroidal rotation and poloidal asymmetries in the
background density) and the neglect of magnetic compression
(B∥fluctuations will be implemented in a new solver under de-
velopment). The quasi-linear approximation relies on a prop-
erty of weak turbulence: the cross-phases between fluctuating
quantities observed in the non-linear regime tend to remain
close to the linear cross-phases. In practice, this means that

III.
COMPARISON OF TGLF LINEAR RESPONSE
AGAINST GYROKINETIC SIMULATIONS (GKW)
In this section, we will compare the linear response of
TGLF against GKW. Our initial focus is on the Waltz stan-
dard case36, a reference scenario with plasma parameters de-
tailed in Table I. We choose to start with this case due to
TGLF’s demonstrated accuracy in modeling the ITG regime,
including electromagnetic β scans37. Our approach involves
beta scans to explore the ITG to KBM transition. These scans
are executed for two different values of the magnetic shear, at
ˆs = 1.0 to examine TGLF under standard conditions, and at
ˆs = 0.05, anticipating low shear conditions met closer to the
magnetic axis of a tokamak. Afterwards, our focus shifts to
the JET hybrid H-mode discharge 75225 to evaluate the accu-
racy of TGLF linear response in the central region of high beta
low magnetic shear plasmas where Kinetic Ballooning Modes
are predicted to be unstable16,18.

A two-stage solution method is used in TGLF. Initially, the
eigenvalues are computed using a smaller number of Hermite
basis functions set by NBASIS_MIN, and this computation is
performed across various wave function widths (θw).
The
width that yields the maximum growth rate is selected for
the subsequent stage, where a larger number of Hermite ba-
sis functions, NBASIS_MAX, is used to obtain the final results.
During the initial stage, TGLF explores values within a range
defined by WIDTH_MIN and WIDTH to determine the optimal
envelope width that maximizes the growth rate.
The NBASIS_MIN and NBASIS_MAX parameters determine
the minimum and maximum number of Hermite basis func-
tions used to solve the wave functions. The default values
are 2 and 4, respectively. We opted for NBASIS_MAX = 6 in-
stead of 4 as it provides more accurate results without notably
increasing the computational cost of the simulations. A de-
tailed investigation of the impact of NBASIS_MAX is presented
in Appendix A.
The WIDTH parameter specifies the maximum width of the
Gaussian envelope used in the Hermite polynomial projection.
In this study, we used a WIDTH value of 3 instead of the default
1.65 to better capture the extended wave functions observed at
low magnetic shear, see Appendix B.
The FILTER input, when set to 0, prevents TGLF from
filtering out high-frequency modes, including KBM modes.
High-frequency spurious modes are sometimes observed in
TGLF simulations. These modes are non-physical and need
to be filtered out. To address this, the FILTER switch was im-
plemented and is recommended by default, with a value of
FILTER = 2. This setting filters out modes with a frequency
higher than twice the drift wave frequency, therefore eliminat-
ing the spurious modes but also KBMs, which are crucial for
our study. To retain KBMs, the FILTER is therefore set to 0.
Later in this paper, a new refined filter will be introduced.
Additionally, all TGLF simulations include perpendicular
magnetic field fluctuations ( B⊥) but exclude parallel magnetic
field fluctuations (B∥). Instead, the setting (USE_MHD_RULE
= True) is used, which forces the ∇B and curvature drifts to
be equal, exploiting a cancellation at the MHD level to ap-
proximate the effect of magnetic compression38,39. Keeping
fluctuations of B∥and set USE_MHD_RULE = False would be
more accurate but is not possible with the present TGLF ver-
sion. An improved linear solver has recently been proposed to
address this issue40.

C.
Jet hybrid H-mode #75225
After evaluating TGLF’s capability to model KBMs in an
idealized scenario represented by the Waltz standard case,
this section extends the benchmark by comparing results from
TGLF and GKW for the JET hybrid H-mode discharge 75225.
This hybrid H-mode discharge, performed when the tokamak
JET featured carbon walls, underwent a detailed analysis in
a previous study18. The discharge is characterized by high-
quality core profile measurements for electrons and main ions,
the absence of sawteeth, and no other significant core MHD
activity within the selected time interval, t = 6.0 −6.5 sec-
onds. The simulation input parameters were derived from a
Gaussian process regression of experimental measurements.
In this section, our investigation centers on modeling this dis-
charge at the two radial positions ρ = 0.15 and ρ = 0.33,
where ρ represents the normalized toroidal flux coordinate.
The relevant local plasma input parameters in the IMAS gy-
rokinetics normalisation34 are detailed in Table II. The values
of β, β ′ and normalised gradients are the self-consistent ex-
perimental values.
The simulations encompass three species: deuterium ions,
electrons and carbon. The linear GKW simulations in this sec-
tion use section III A settings with Npol = 49. This increase
from 29 to 49 poloidal turns is necessary for the JET case due
to the presence of more extended wavefunctions. TGLF simu-
lations follow the same settings as in section III A. By default,
TGLF sets the FILTER parameter to 2, which automatically
removes any modes with frequencies exceeding twice the drift

non-physical modes, it also excludes genuine high-frequency
modes such as KBMs. This feature was therefore disabled un-
til now by setting FILTER = 0. However, this significantly in-
creases the risk of incorrect spurious modes slipping through,

COMPARISON OF TGLF QUASI-LINEAR FLUXES
AGAINST GYROKINETIC NONLINEAR SIMULATIONS
In this section, we compare the quasi-linear flux predictions
from TGLF with those obtained from nonlinear simulations
conducted using the gyrokinetic code GKW. This compari-
son focuses on modeling the central region of the JET 75225


8
discharge at the radial position ρ = 0.15. The quasi-linear
weights have been validated in the previous section, allowing
us to now focus on the quasi-linear saturation model.
A.
Codes Setup
1.
Non-linear GKW Setup Parameters
All nonlinear GKW simulations are conducted with the fol-
lowing grid parameters: Ny = 16 binormal modes, Nx = 261
radial modes, Ns = 32 parallel grid points, Nµ = 16 magnetic
moments and Nv∥= 48 parallel velocity grid points. The krρs
and kθρs grids are defined by |krρs|min = 0.044, |krρs|max =
5.73, kθρs|min= 0.08, and kθρs|max= 1.25. The time step size
is set to DTIM = 0.00015 in normalized GKW units.
Nu-
merical dissipation is applied with the following coefficients:
disp_par = 0.9 for parallel derivatives, disp_x = 3.0 for
the radial direction, and disp_y = 0.1 for the binormal di-
rection.
Numerical dissipation in the parallel direction is
needed to avoid numerical instability. The applied level has
been checked to not significantly alter the linear growth rates.
Numerical dissipation in the perpendicular direction is used
to avoid spectral pile-up at the higher krρs and kθρs values
as customary in local delta-f gyrokinetic codes. The physics
settings are the same as for the linear simulations but the simu-
lations now include four species: deuterium, electrons, carbon
and fast ions, whereas the linear simulations focused on three
species (deuterium, electrons and carbon).
2.
Quasi-linear TGLF Setup Parameters
The TGLF simulations are set up based on the results from
the linear analysis, with FILTER = −1.5 and WIDTH = 3 to
better capture KBMs. The quasi-linear saturation model is
SAT_RULE = 2. TGLF includes four distinct saturation mod-
els to approximate turbulence saturation.
For this study,
SAT_RULE = 2 was selected as it is the most widely used in
the community. The KYGRID_MODEL parameter is set to 1,
which adapts the wavenumber grid so that the minimum kθρs
is 0.1. This is in contrast to the grid with KYGRID_MODEL = 4,
where the minimum kθρs would be 0.05. KYGRID_MODEL = 1
is recommended to avoid issues associated with very low kθρs
values.
In TGLF, the local maximum of the γ/kθρs spectrum plays
a critical role in the application of the saturation models,
which rely on two key values extracted from the γ/kθρs curve:
• kθ,maxρs: The binormal wavenumber (kθρs) at which
the ratio γ/kθρs reaches its local maximum.
• γmax: The linear growth rate at kθ,maxρs.
For very low kθρs values, even a small overestimation of the
linear growth rate γ can cause the ratio γ/kθρs to reach its
local maximum in this region, leading to an inaccurate iden-
tification of kθ,maxρs and γmax.
To address this limitation,
the parameter ALPHA_ZF is used to exclude very low kθρs
values from consideration when identifying γ/kθρs|max. If
ALPHA_ZF is set to a negative value (the default value is 0),
the minimum kθ,minρs considered for the search of the peak is
adjusted to kθ,minρs = 0.173
√
2. This adjustment prevents ex-
cessively high predicted saturation levels that may result from
spurious peaks at very low kθρs values. To further improve
precision, a quadratic interpolation is applied around the iden-
tified maximum using three consecutive points in the γ/kθρs
spectrum. This interpolation refines both γmax and kθ,maxρs.
An important detail is that the refined values derived from
the interpolation may not correspond to a point in the origi-
nal kθρs spectrum grid. In such cases, while TGLF accurately
computes these maximum values, the turbulent fluxes at these
interpolated points will not be evaluated. Although the param-
eter ALPHA_ZF does not impact the linear response, it plays
a crucial role in estimating the non-linear saturation level of
turbulent fluxes. However, it is an ad-hoc adjustment intro-
duced to address limitations in the TGLF saturation model,
underscoring the need for caution when interpreting results,
especially when modeling Kinetic Ballooning Modes, where
the peak of γ/kθρs often occurs at the lowest kθρs values
due to the presence of unstable modes at very low binormal
wavenumber.

quasi-linear flux predictions against the nonlinear fluxes com-
puted with the gyrokinetic code GKW in the central region of
the JET #75225 discharge. The primary aim was to assess the
accuracy of TGLF in high-beta low magnetic shear regimes,

TGLF linear response was first validated for the reference
Waltz standard case, establishing its baseline accuracy in cap-
turing the essential physics of KBMs. The analysis showed
that TGLF effectively models KBMs under standard condi-
tions but encounters difficulties at very low magnetic shear
values near the ITG-KBM transition.
The study then focused on the JET hybrid H-mode dis-
charge #75225. Results demonstrated that while TGLF could
reasonably capture the linear growth rates and mode struc-
tures, discrepancies arise in the low-binormal wavevector re-
gion, which is critical for accurately predicting quasi-linear
fluxes. To address these limitations, a new filtering mech-
anism was developed and implemented within the TGLF
framework. This filter, designed to retain modes with even
parity in the electrostatic potential while excluding non-
physical spurious modes, significantly enhanced TGLF’s abil-
ity to accurately model KBMs.
The quasi-linear flux predictions from TGLF were then
compared to the nonlinear fluxes from GKW. By systemati-
cally analyzing various TGLF settings, we identified an opti-
mized configuration for modeling KBMs. Our findings high-
light the sensitivity of TGLF’s performance to its parameter
settings and underscore the importance of careful parameter
selection. The optimized TGLF settings in Table IV offer a
baseline for modeling KBMs.
However, their robustness across other scenarios requires
further validation and testing. Although these settings are de-
signed for broad applicability, they can be restrictive in certain
cases, potentially excluding relevant modes.
Using the new filter and optimized settings, TGLF’s flux
predictions were compared to GKW nonlinear simulations for
ion and electron heat and particle fluxes.
The Root Mean
Square (RMS) average errors were 67.0% for the ion parti-
cle flux (Γi), 45.6% for the electron particle flux (Γe), 75.9%
for the ion heat flux (Qi), and 64.7% for the electron heat
flux (Qe). TGLF was found to underestimate the electron heat
flux. This discrepancy arises from the strong underestimation
of the magnetic flutter contribution to the electron heat flux by
TGLF. A proposed explanation for this underestimation is that
this magnetic flutter contribution not captured by TGLF, may
result from the non-linear excitation of sub-dominant micro-
tearing modes as suggested in18, and would require further
development of quasi-linear models to be accounted for. For
the electrosatic part, as long as the linear response is properly
captured, TGLF saturation model provides a correct predic-
tion of the non-linear fluxes in the KBM regime.
A parameter scan in R/LTe and R/LTi confirmed that TGLF
captures the trends with respect to temperature gradients ob-
served in GKW non-linear simulations. This validation rein-
forces the potential of TGLF for integrated modeling frame-
works.
In summary, this study highlights both the strengths and
limitations of TGLF in modeling turbulent transport in high-
beta plasmas. The development of the new filtering mecha-
nism and the identification of optimized settings offer a robust
baseline for KBM studies, balancing accuracy and computa-
tional efficiency. The underestimation of magnetic flutter con-
tributions indicates a need for further refinement in TGLF’s
electromagnetic treatment.
Future research should focus on improving the electromag-
netic modeling within TGLF, building upon the new linear
solver developed in Ref40, and validating the optimized set-
tings across a broader range of plasma scenarios. These efforts
will be crucial for enhancing the reliability and robustness of
TGLF in predicting turbulent transport in diverse high-beta
plasma conditions.

Appendix D: New Filter in TGLF
The newly implemented filter in TGLF addresses the chal-
lenge of distinguishing between kinetic ballooning modes and
spurious modes. The primary goal is to accurately capture the
KBMs while effectively filtering out spurious modes. This
section details the methodology and effectiveness of the new
filter.
1.
Methodology
The initial filtering methodology in TGLF involves filter-
ing out any mode with a frequency ωr that exceeds a speci-
fied multiple of the drift wave frequency ωDW. This multiple
correspond to the value provided in the TGLF input param-
eter FILTER and by default its value is set to 2. This ap-
proach removes spurious high-frequency modes but also ex-
cludes KBMs, which are characterized by high frequencies.
The observation that TGLF spurious high-frequency modes
tend to have an odd parity along the field line whereas KBMs
have even parity motivated the development of a new filtering
mechanism. The steps involved are:
• Frequency Check:
The filter compares the real part of the mode frequency
ωr with the drift wave frequency ωDW. If |ωr| exceeds a
specified multiple of |ωDW|, additional checks are per-
formed. Note that this multiple correspond to the value
provided in the TGLF input parameter FILTER.
• Parity Check:
For high-frequency modes that goes though the fre-
quency check, the real part of the electrostatic potential
ℜ(φ) is examined for parity. Modes with high frequen-
cies that are even and propagates in the ion diamagnetic
drift direction are identified as KBMs and are not fil-
tered out. All other modes that do not meet these con-
ditions are recognized as spurious and are filtered out.
The mode structure in TGLF are projected on a basis of
Hermite functions (see Appendix A). To determine the parity
of the mode, we use the properties of the basis Hermite func-
tions, where odd-indexed Hermite polynomials correspond to
even functions of the parallel direction θ, and even-indexed
Hermite polynomials correspond to odd functions. We con-
struct a function with the same parity as the electrostatic po-
tential φ and evaluate its parity by calculating the ratio of the
absolute value of its sum to the sum of its absolute values.
Modes with a ratio higher than 0.9 are classified as even.
Test on the robustness of the even parity evaluation
To test the robustness of the new filtering technique, we in-
creased the parallel velocity shear to alter the parity of the
KBM mode structure.
The parity check for the filter was
found to remain effective except in rare cases where the mode
structure was extremely uneven. In these instances, the ratio
between the absolute value of the sum and the sum of the ab-
solute values is around 0.5, making it difficult to adjust the
filter threshold reliably. Out of 441 test cases varying kθρs
and the parallel velocity shear, 5 cases exhibited this parity
check issue and were not recognized as KBMs, resulting in
their exclusion.

The robustness of the new filter has been tested to ensure
that it does not exclude physically relevant modes with odd
structures in the real part of the electrostatic potential. The
filtering procedure applies the parity test only to modes with
frequencies above FILTER × ωDW. For physical modes, their
frequencies are expected to lie below this threshold, meaning
they bypass the parity check and are not filtered out. On the
other hand, if a mode has a frequency above FILTER × ωDW,
it would already be excluded by the default filtering mecha-
nism in TGLF, regardless of its structure. Therefore, the new
filtering method does not remove any physical modes that the
original filtering would have kept.
The exact mechanism behind the generation of spurious
modes in TGLF remains unclear but appears to stem from
the numerical implementation of its eigensolver. Tests indi-
cate that these modes are more likely to arise when modeling
plasmas with low aspect ratio. A new eigensolver (GFS) for
TGLF40, which incorporates the effects of parallel magnetic
fields and offers improved handling of KBMs, is expected to
be released soon. The filter developed in this work serves as a
temporary solution to mitigate the current solver’s limitations
